# POA vs. Durable Power of Attorney on a Checking Account

**Power of Attorney (POA) - General/Standard**
A standard POA gives someone (the "agent" or "attorney-in-fact") authority to act on your behalf regarding your checking account—writing checks, making withdrawals, managing transactions, etc. However, this authority **automatically ends if you become mentally incapacitated** (or, in some versions, at a specified time or event). It's meant to be used while you're fully capable of making decisions but perhaps unavailable (traveling, deployed, etc.).

**Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA)**
A durable POA includes the same authority to manage your checking account, but with one critical difference: it **remains valid even if you become incapacitated** due to illness, injury, or cognitive decline (like dementia). The "durable" designation specifically means the power *survives* your incapacity—it's built to last through the exact situation where you'd need someone to step in and manage your finances because you no longer can.

## Key Practical Difference

| Feature | Standard POA | Durable POA |
|---|---|---|
| Valid while you're competent | Yes | Yes |
| Valid if you become incapacitated | **No** – automatically terminates | **Yes** – continues |
| Common use | Temporary convenience (travel, short-term help) | Long-term planning, elder care, disability protection |

## Why This Matters for a Checking Account

If you only have a standard POA and you become incapacitated (say, from a stroke or advanced dementia), your agent **loses the ability to access your checking account right when you need help most**—often forcing family members into court to get guardianship/conservatorship, which is costly and slow.

With a **durable** POA, the named agent can continue paying bills, managing deposits, and handling the account seamlessly, without interruption, regardless of your mental state.

## Bottom Line
Most financial and estate planning attorneys recommend using a **durable** power of attorney for bank accounts specifically *because* it protects against the scenario of incapacity—which is often the very reason someone sets up a POA in the first place. Banks will typically ask whether the POA document includes durability language, since it affects whether they'll honor the agent's authority long-term.
